The radar-absorbing material (RAM) used in the study showed more than -10 dB reflection loss from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies.

Three different rivet configurations were studied: (a) rivet installed at the center of the unit cell (RAS C1), (b) rivet installed between the gap of two unit cells (RAS C2), and (c) rivet installed at the center of four unit cells (RAS C3).
The study considered three cases with varying the percentage of rivet heads area to RAS surface area: (a) 9.8%, (b) 4.4%, and (c) 2.5%.
The RAS C1 configuration showed the worst RCS performance, with up to 10 dB degradation, while the RAS C3 configuration showed the best performance among the three rivet configurations.
As the rivet surface area decreased from 9.8% to 4.4% and 2.5%, the degradation in RCS performance also decreased, with the 2.5% case showing a maximum of 3 dB degradation.
The study evaluated air intake ducts with varying lengths: 1.0 m, 2.0 m, 4.0 m, 6.0 m, and 8.0 m. Longer ducts (4.0 m and above) showed better median RCS reduction compared to the shorter ducts.

For the open-source aircraft CAD model, all the RAS configurations with and without rivets showed similar RCS performance, with approximately 10 dB RCS reduction from 4 to 18 GHz of frequencies compared to the non-RAS (PEC) air intake duct.
The RAS configuration considered in the study showed degrading performance below 4 GHz, as it was optimized for the 4 to 18 GHz frequency range.
The circular air intake ducts showed much higher RCS reduction compared to the aircraft-level RCS, due to the contribution of other aircraft components and systems to the overall RCS.
The paper highlights the importance of examining all structural elements, including fasteners, which can become dominant contributors to the RCS of low-observable aircraft designs.

The study considered a simplified case of rivets, and a more detailed study on the impact of different shapes, sizes, and patterns of rivets on the RCS performance of a low-observable aircraft would be an open research area.
The impact of rivets on a low-observable aircraft model, as opposed to the open-source model used in this study, will be an area of future research.

The paper mentions that maintenance and damage detection are essential for long-term stealth performance, and a dual modality detection system combining visual and microwave imaging can be used to assess damage in radar-absorbing materials.

The analysis of the electromagnetic scattering of rivets on the conducting plane using Electric Field Integral Equation (EFIE) and the RCS effect of rivets on a plate with incident angle were studied in previous research.
Fasteners may introduce significant RCS challenges for a stealth aircraft, and precise measurement and analysis of these weak scattering sources are critical for optimizing stealth performance.
